source.title: IsoCompute Playbook: Optimally Scaling Sampling Compute for LLM RL
source.authors: Zhou-Jun Cheng; Yutao Xie; Yu-Xiao Qu; Amrith Rajagopal Setlur; Shi-Bo Hao; Varad Pimpalkhute; Tong-Tong Liang; Feng Yao; Zheng-Zhong Liu; E. Xing; Virginia Smith; Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Zhiting Hu; Taylor W. Killian; Aviral Kumar

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends compute-allocation scaling analysis to LLM RL post-training, but its results concern rollout allocation and reward, not the claim’s pretraining cross-entropy laws or parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports empirical RL sampling-compute allocation results, but does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, power-law loss versus parameters/tokens/compute, or compute-optimal parameter and token counts. Its RL findings are recorded under fits_no_version; they do not test the listed versions. The paper also cites pretraining scaling laws as motivation, which is not a result row.
record.test_reason: The study fits sigmoids for compute-optimal RL rollout allocation (n, Bp, M) against validation reward in LLM RL post-training. It measures no pretraining loss and no parameter or token scaling, and fits no power-law loss form in any regime. It cites pretraining scaling laws and Chinchilla only as motivation and analogy. Its results therefore bear on no listed version. T6 fits better than the reader's T3, because T3 requires a result on the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the compute-optimal rollouts per problem rise with sampling compute and saturate, while problems per batch acts mainly as a stability knob. They also find the behaviour depends on the base model, prompt distribution and evaluation metric.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies on-policy RL post-training allocation across rollout count, problem batch size, and update steps, using reward metrics and sigmoid fits. It does not use the original studies’ pretraining loss measurements or parameter/token compute-optimal fitting recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The allocation trend and saturation point vary with problem difficulty, dataset size, base model, evaluation metric, algorithm, and compute constraints. The hard-set fixed-batch n*(M) trend is non-monotonic; small training sets can cause validation overfitting.

fits_no_version.finding: For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, compute-optimal rollouts per problem n*(C) rise with RL sampling compute and then saturate, fitted by a sigmoid. Saturation comes earlier on Hard problems.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LLM RL post-training, compute-optimal rollouts per problem rise with sampling compute, then saturate depending on difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: Under a fixed total batch size, Easy-set n*(M) is sigmoidal while the Hard-set trend is non-monotonic. Reward is far more sensitive to n than to Bp on Easy, but comparable on Hard.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL allocation between per-problem rollouts and problems per batch depends on task difficulty.

fits_no_version.finding: A small training set (D=500) caps the optimal n at 256, and n=512 degrades validation reward. Other base models show different saturation points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL compute-optimal rollout range depends on dataset size and base model, with overfitting at small data.

fits_no_version.finding: The preference for larger n at high compute appears under PPO and CISPO and on AIME24. The gain is attributed to exploration rather than baseline variance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The RL rollout-scaling trend generalizes across algorithms and is driven by exploration.

fits_no_version.finding: The compute-optimal n depends on the target metric (best@4 vs worst@4). The n* sigmoid is near-identical when compute is counted in tokens rather than rollouts, though the slope k differs (Figs 8, 20, 24).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL allocation fits depend on the evaluation metric but are robust to the choice of compute unit.

record.problems: The results concern RL rollout-based reward and allocation, not pretraining cross-entropy loss. Several figures are described qualitatively without exact values or uncertainty estimates. The authors note limited sweep ranges and that extremely large combined Bp and n regimes were not explored; they also did not extensively retune hyperparameters for PPO and CISPO.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Some figures provide further frontier curves and training-reward distributions, but their qualitative results are represented by the main text findings above.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation of loss from small to large runs. Its n*(C) sigmoid fits concern RL allocation, not loss.
No parameter/token compute-optimal split. Allocation is over rollouts, problems per batch and update steps.
RL post-training regime studied, but no power-law loss form is tested. Reward curves and allocation are fitted with sigmoids.
AIME24 gains with larger n are not related to model scale or pretraining loss.
Setup-dependence concerns RL allocation rules, not pretraining exponents or the parameter/token split.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly linked to none. Row states are judged against the paper's own n-scaling expectation, not any claim version. The study's sigmoid fits are of RL reward/allocation, not loss power laws, so it cannot inform V5 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss scaling against parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict the loss of substantially larger pretraining runs.
The study optimizes RL rollout, problem-batch, and update-step allocation; it does not measure compute-optimal parameter and token counts.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
Although the setting is RL post-training, the study does not test whether the same power-law loss form holds in that regime; its outcomes are RL reward and rollout-allocation trends.
The study reports some downstream task results, but does not test downstream performance as a predictable function of pretraining loss or scale.
The study finds setup-dependent RL allocation trends, but does not test whether the published pretraining loss exponents or parameter/token compute-optimal split depend on fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Swept parallel rollouts per problem n against sampling compute with Bp = 32; measured validation avg@4.
rows.measure: Validation reward (avg@4) and compute-optimal n as a function of rollout compute.
rows.value: The compute-optimal n increases with compute and is well-approximated by a sigmoid; the frontier saturates, and n = 512 continues to dominate at high compute.
rows.note: This is an RL reward/allocation result, not a pretraining loss scaling result.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Swept n against sampling compute with Bp = 32; measured validation avg@4.
rows.measure: Validation reward (avg@4) and compute-optimal n as a function of rollout compute.
rows.value: The compute-optimal n increases with compute and saturates at a smaller value than on Easy; n = 512 yields lower final performance and is not on the compute-optimal frontier.
rows.note: The increasing trend is qualified by earlier saturation and a lower-performing large-n setting.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared allocations between n and Bp under a fixed total batch size B = 8,192 while varying sequential iterations M.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal n and Bp as functions of M.
rows.value: n*(M) has a sigmoidal dependence on M; the corresponding optimal Bp decreases according to an inverse sigmoid.
rows.note: This is allocation among RL sampling dimensions, not parameter/token allocation.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared allocations between n and Bp under a fixed total batch size while varying M.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal n and Bp as functions of M.
rows.value: The compute-optimal n has a non-monotonic dependence on M; the optimal Bp trend is correspondingly irregular.
rows.note: The study explicitly contrasts this result with the cleaner Easy-set trend.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation reward sensitivity to changes in Bp and n.
rows.measure: Reported reward range when varying each allocation dimension.
rows.value: Varying n: 9.2% range; varying Bp: 1.9% range.
rows.note: The text says the n effect is clearly positive and substantially larger than the Bp effect.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation reward sensitivity to changes in Bp and n.
rows.measure: Reported reward range when varying each allocation dimension.
rows.value: Varying Bp: 2.2% range; varying n: 3.1% range.
rows.note: The paper describes the effects as comparable and the Bp trend as fluctuating.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Jointly swept Bp, n, and M under fixed total rollout-compute budgets.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal n*(C) and performance sensitivity to Bp.
rows.value: n*(C) increases monotonically with compute and is well-fit by a sigmoid; performance varies only weakly with Bp within a moderate range.
rows.note: The reported scaling variable is RL rollout allocation, not model parameters or pretraining tokens.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Jointly swept Bp, n, and M under fixed total rollout-compute budgets.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal n*(C) and performance sensitivity to Bp.
rows.value: n*(C) increases monotonically with compute and is well-fit by a sigmoid; performance varies only weakly with Bp within a moderate range.
rows.note: The paper notes that extremely large total rollout sizes with both Bp and n large were not explored.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal rollout allocations across training-set sizes.
rows.note: The authors compare this with the smaller-data condition.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared compute-optimal rollout allocations across training-set sizes.
rows.value: The frontier saturates at n = 256; scaling to n = 512 degrades performance, which the paper attributes to overfitting.
rows.note: The degradation is reported for validation performance.

rows.subject: Qwen3-4B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation reward across rollout counts at increasing compute.
rows.value: Larger n values outperform the n = 8 baseline at high compute; the optimal n varies across model–dataset pairs.
rows.note: The text reports the result across Easy and Hard settings in aggregate; exact figure values are not stated.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation reward across rollout counts at increasing compute.
rows.value: Larger n values outperform the n = 8 baseline at high compute; validation reward saturates or degrades at n = 128 even as training reward continues to rise.
rows.note: The authors attribute the training–validation divergence to overfitting.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated models trained with varying n on the AIME24 downstream task.
rows.value: Larger n leads to higher performance.
rows.note: The text gives no exact scores and does not relate the result to pretraining loss.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the n-sweep protocol under PPO.
rows.value: Larger n yields consistently better performance at matched compute.
rows.note: The study says it did not extensively retune hyperparameters for each algorithm.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the n-sweep protocol under PPO.
rows.value: Earlier saturation and weaker separation among large n values.
rows.note: The paper describes this as consistent with the Easy regime being less exploration-limited.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Repeated the n-sweep protocol under CISPO.
rows.value: Smooth learning curves and competitive performance from moderate-to-large n as compute grows.
rows.note: The text reports a qualitative pattern rather than exact values.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared full large-n training, small-n training, and high-precision baseline estimation with a subsampled policy-gradient update.
rows.baseline: Small n = 64/64 and decoupled 64/256 perform approximately equally.
rows.value: Large n = 256/256 performs best; ordering reported as (1) > (3) ≈ (2).
rows.note: The authors conclude that lower-variance baseline estimation gives negligible gains in this setting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
